title: Office Application Startup: Outlook Rules
summary: Outlook rules are server side instructions that the mailbox applies to incoming mail automatically, such as moving a message to a folder or running a script when a message matches a condition. The scripting action that rules once supported is the abuse path here: a rule created with a script action, or with an action that launches an external program, runs in the user context as messages are processed, and it does so whether or not the user is watching the screen. Rules replicate with the mailbox, so the persistence point is the mailbox rather than the endpoint, and it survives a rebuild of the workstation. Two distinct behaviours appear in the wild: a hidden rule that quietly moves replies out of the Inbox so the attacker can read them, and a rule whose script action downloads or starts a payload when a specific message arrives. The durable artefacts are the rule definition in the mailbox, the mailbox audit record of the rule being created or modified, and the process or network activity that the rule action produces on the workstation. Legitimate rules are extremely common, so the discriminator is content and shape: rules that include a script action, rules hidden from the client, rules named to blend in with defaults, and rules whose only purpose is to delete or forward messages containing security keywords.

beginner.definition: An Outlook rule is an automatic instruction, for example move any message from this sender into that folder. This technique is when an attacker adds a rule to your mailbox that runs hidden code or hides their own email from you.
beginner.whyItMatters: Rules live in your mailbox, so they keep working on any computer you sign in to. Because rules are normal and common, one extra rule is easy to miss. A rule can also carry out actions, such as starting a program, whenever the right message arrives.
howItWorks: Outlook lets you create rules that act on mail automatically as it arrives.
One rule action type can run a script or start another program.
The attacker creates such a rule in your mailbox, often with a boring name.
The rule is stored in the mailbox and loads again every time Outlook starts.
When a matching message arrives, the action runs without you clicking anything.
Some rules instead move or delete messages, keeping warnings away from you.
beginner.example: Imagine a hotel front desk with a rule book. A guest adds one line: whenever a letter arrives for room twelve, deliver it to locker nine instead. The staff follow the book perfectly and the guest collects the letters himself. Nobody broke a lock and the letter was never lost.
takeaways: Rules are stored in the mailbox, so they survive a new laptop.
A rule with a script or program action is unusual and worth investigating.
Check for rules that are hidden from the client or that delete security alerts.

objectives: Explain what an Outlook rule is and which rule actions can lead to code execution.
Describe how this sub-technique differs from the parent technique Office Application Startup.
Describe how a rule persists in the mailbox and triggers when a matching message arrives.
Identify the mailbox audit events and client artefacts that expose rule creation.
Distinguish an attacker created rule from ordinary mail sorting rules.
